# Introduction

- Structural equation modeling (SEM) is widely used in psychology and the social sciences because it allows researchers to evaluate and modify theoretical models.

- Anderson and Gerbing explain that although SEM has strong potential for theory development, its complexity can also create problems when researchers do not apply it carefully.

- The main purpose of the article is to provide practical guidance for using SEM in theory testing and development.

- The authors recommend a two-step modeling approach that separates the evaluation of the measurement model from the evaluation of the structural model.

- The measurement model explains how observed measures relate to their underlying latent constructs.

- The structural model explains the hypothesized relationships among the latent constructs.

- The authors argue that the measurement model should be evaluated and, if necessary, respecified before the measurement and structural components are estimated together.

- This separation helps researchers make more meaningful conclusions about theoretical constructs and reduces the possibility of misleading interpretations.

- The measurement model is especially important for evaluating convergent validity and discriminant validity.

- After acceptable measurement has been established, the structural model can be used to evaluate the hypothesized relationships among constructs and provide evidence related to nomological validity.

# Background

## Exploratory Versus Confirmatory Analyses

- Anderson and Gerbing explain that exploratory and confirmatory analysis should not always be treated as completely separate categories.

- Instead, research can be viewed as moving along a progression from more exploratory analysis toward more confirmatory analysis.

- In exploratory factor analysis, researchers may begin without specifying the number of factors in advance.

- The analysis becomes more confirmatory when researchers specify the expected number of factors and evaluate how well that factor structure fits the data.

- In confirmatory factor analysis, researchers specify the measurement model in advance, including which observed variables are expected to measure particular latent constructs.

- Even a confirmatory model may require respecification when the initial model does not fit the data adequately.

- Because researchers often revise and reestimate models using the same sample, the process is not always purely confirmatory.

- A stronger confirmatory test occurs when the final model is cross-validated using a different sample from the same population.

- Cross-validation provides stronger evidence that the final model is not simply fitting characteristics that are unique to the original sample.

## Complementary Approaches for Theory Testing Versus Predictive Application

- The authors distinguish between using SEM for theory testing and development and using SEM for prediction.

- For theory testing and development, they discuss full-information estimation methods such as maximum likelihood (ML) and generalized least squares (GLS).

- ML and GLS are used with the common factor model, which separates theoretically meaningful construct variance from random measurement error and measure-specific variance.

- Full-information methods are useful for theory testing because they provide efficient parameter estimates and an overall test of model fit.

- For predictive applications, the authors discuss partial least squares (PLS).

- PLS focuses more heavily on maximizing explained variance and predicting scores than on testing a complete theoretical model.

- A limitation of PLS is that it does not directly assess unidimensional measurement in the same way as the confirmatory factor-analysis approach.

- PLS also does not provide an overall test of model fit.

- The authors therefore describe the approaches as complementary rather than competing.

- Their general position is that ML or GLS is more appropriate for theory testing and development, while PLS can be more useful for prediction and application.

- Because the article focuses on theory testing and development, the remainder of the article emphasizes a confirmatory two-step approach using ML or GLS.

## Estimation Methods

- Maximum likelihood (ML) had become the most commonly used estimation method in structural equation modeling.

- Under the assumption of multivariate normality, ML estimators have desirable large-sample properties, including being unbiased, consistent, and efficient.

- ML also allows researchers to test the statistical significance of individual parameters and evaluate overall model fit using the chi-square statistic.

- A limitation of normal-theory ML is that its standard errors and chi-square test can be affected when the data violate the assumption of multivariate normality.

- Because of these limitations, researchers developed more general estimation approaches that relax the normality assumption.

- Generalized least squares (GLS) methods estimate model parameters by minimizing a weighted function of the differences between observed and model-predicted covariances.

- Different GLS methods can be created depending on how the weighting matrix is specified.

- Asymptotically distribution-free (ADF) methods were developed to provide estimates that do not require the assumption of multivariate normality.

- ADF methods are more flexible, but they can require very large samples and much greater computational resources.

- The article also discusses approximation methods designed to reduce the computational burden of full ADF estimation, including linearized estimation and diagonally weighted least squares.

- Elliptical estimation provides another alternative by allowing variables to have a shared nonzero kurtosis rather than requiring strict multivariate normality.

- The authors note that these newer estimation methods were important theoretical advances, but they also involved practical trade-offs related to sample size and computation.

- The choice of estimation method should depend on the characteristics of the data and the assumptions that can reasonably be made.

- The authors suggest that researchers should evaluate whether multivariate normality is reasonable before choosing between normal-theory and more general estimation methods.

# Confirmatory Measurement Model

- A confirmatory measurement model specifies the relationships between observed variables and the latent constructs they are intended to measure.

- In this model, the latent constructs are allowed to correlate freely with one another.

- The observed measures are connected to the latent constructs through factor loadings.

- The model also includes measurement error and variance that is specific to individual measures.

- The purpose of the confirmatory measurement model is to evaluate whether the observed indicators represent the intended theoretical constructs in an acceptable way.

- Anderson and Gerbing treat the measurement model as a separate part of the SEM process because researchers need to establish adequate measurement before interpreting structural relationships among constructs.

## Need for Unidimensional Measurement

- Anderson and Gerbing describe unidimensional measurement as an important requirement for theory testing and development.

- Unidimensionality means that a set of indicators has one underlying trait or construct in common.

- Establishing unidimensionality is necessary before researchers can assign a clear theoretical meaning to an estimated latent construct.

- The authors discuss two criteria for evaluating unidimensionality: internal consistency and external consistency.

- Internal consistency refers to whether indicators of the same construct relate to one another in a way that is consistent with a single underlying factor.

- External consistency concerns whether the relationships between indicators of one construct and indicators of another construct are consistent with the proposed measurement structure.

- Multiple-indicator measurement models are preferred because they allow constructs to be defined by more than one observed measure.

- In a preferred multiple-indicator model, each indicator is intended to measure only one construct.

- When indicators load on several constructs or when correlated measurement errors are introduced, the measures are no longer clearly unidimensional.

- Losing unidimensionality can make it harder to interpret the theoretical meaning of the latent constructs.

- The authors recognize that some individual items may be more complex than a simple one-factor representation suggests.

- They note that higher-order factors or composites can sometimes be used when the constructs of interest are broader than the first-order factors represented by individual items.

## Specification

- The authors explain that the measurement model must be properly specified before researchers can meaningfully evaluate its fit.

- One important specification decision is how to set the metric, or scale, of the latent factors.

- Anderson and Gerbing recommend fixing the factor variances to 1.0 rather than fixing one factor loading per construct to 1.0.

- Setting factor variances to 1.0 allows researchers to test whether each factor loading is statistically significant.

- The authors strongly prefer using multiple indicators for each latent construct whenever possible.

- In some cases, however, researchers may have only one indicator for a construct.

- When a construct has only a single indicator, researchers must make assumptions about the indicator’s measurement error because the error cannot be estimated in the same way as it can with multiple indicators.

- Ideally, the error variance for a single indicator should come from prior research or another independent source.

- If no independent estimate is available, the researcher must make a judgment about the error variance, although the authors note that this introduces some arbitrariness.

- Sample size is also an important part of model specification and estimation.

- The authors report that relatively small samples can sometimes produce unbiased parameter estimates, but estimates may still be too unstable for practical interpretation.

- They note that sample sizes around 150 or more are often needed to obtain parameter estimates with sufficiently small standard errors for practical use.

- Smaller samples are more likely to produce nonconvergence or improper solutions.

- Models with only two indicators per factor can be especially difficult and may require larger samples.

- More complex estimation methods, such as asymptotically distribution-free methods, may require much larger sample sizes than normal-theory maximum likelihood estimation.

## Assessment of Fit

- After estimating the measurement model, researchers should evaluate how well the model fits the observed data.

- Anderson and Gerbing discuss several goodness-of-fit measures, including the chi-square likelihood ratio test, the goodness-of-fit index, and the root-mean-square residual.

- Overall fit statistics help researchers determine whether the proposed measurement model provides an acceptable representation of the data.

- Convergent validity can be evaluated by examining whether each indicator has a statistically significant factor loading on its intended construct.

- A significant factor loading suggests that the indicator is meaningfully related to the construct it is supposed to measure.

- Discriminant validity concerns whether two constructs are sufficiently distinct from one another.

- The authors describe a chi-square difference test in which the correlation between two constructs is constrained to 1.0 and compared with a model in which the correlation is freely estimated.

- If the unconstrained model fits significantly better, this supports the conclusion that the two constructs are not perfectly correlated and therefore show discriminant validity.

- A second way to assess discriminant validity is to examine whether the confidence interval around the estimated correlation between two constructs includes 1.0.

- The authors recommend evaluating pairs of constructs individually rather than testing many pairs simultaneously because problems involving one pair could otherwise be hidden by stronger results from other pairs.

## Respecification

- Anderson and Gerbing recognize that measurement models often need to be respecified when the initial model does not fit adequately.

- Respecification should not be based only on statistical results.

- Researchers should also rely on theory and the substantive meaning of the constructs when deciding how to modify a model.

- Using theory helps reduce the number of alternative models that need to be considered and reduces the risk of changing a model only to take advantage of random characteristics of the sample.

- Nonconvergence and improper solutions may indicate problems with the model specification or characteristics of the sample.

- Possible respecification strategies include assigning an indicator to a different factor or removing a problematic indicator.

- The authors identify four basic ways to modify indicators: move an indicator to another factor, remove it, allow it to load on multiple factors, or correlate measurement errors.

- The first two options are generally preferred because they can preserve unidimensional measurement.

- Allowing cross-loadings or correlated measurement errors may improve statistical fit but can reduce interpretability and theoretical meaning.

- Correlated measurement errors should generally be specified only when there is a clear theoretical reason for expecting them.

- Residual patterns can help identify indicators that may be incorrectly assigned or multidimensional.

- The authors recommend combining statistical information, residual analysis, and substantive theory when making respecification decisions.

- A model may sometimes be judged acceptable even when the chi-square statistic remains significant, particularly when other fit indices and residual patterns indicate reasonable fit.

# One-Step Versus Two-Step Modeling Approaches

- The central argument of the article is that researchers gain important advantages by evaluating and respecifying the measurement model before estimating the measurement and structural models together.

- A one-step approach estimates the measurement and structural components simultaneously.

- A two-step approach first evaluates the adequacy of the measurement model and then evaluates the hypothesized structural relationships.

- Separating the two stages allows researchers to determine more clearly whether poor model fit comes from measurement problems or from the proposed structural relationships.

- The two-step approach also reduces the possibility that good fit in one part of the model will hide poor fit in another part.

## The Confirmatory Structural Model

- The confirmatory structural model represents the hypothesized relationships among latent constructs.

- Unlike the measurement model, which focuses on relationships between indicators and constructs, the structural model focuses on relationships among the constructs themselves.

- Structural models distinguish between endogenous and exogenous constructs.

- Endogenous constructs have their causes represented within the model.

- Exogenous constructs have causes that lie outside the model and are not the main focus of the analysis.

- The structural component and the measurement components can be estimated simultaneously once acceptable measurement has been established.

- One major concern with estimating everything at once is interpretational confounding.

- Interpretational confounding occurs when the empirical meaning of a latent construct changes depending on how the structural relationships are specified.

- This can be observed when factor-loading estimates change substantially across different structural models.

- Estimating the measurement model separately first reduces the possibility of interpretational confounding.

- If unidimensional measurement has been established, factor loadings should change very little when alternative structural models are estimated.

## Recommended Two-Step Modeling Approach

### Step 1: Evaluate the Measurement Model

- The first step is to estimate and evaluate the confirmatory measurement model.

- The measurement model examines how observed indicators relate to the latent constructs they are intended to measure.

- Researchers first determine whether the indicators provide acceptable measurement of the constructs before examining the hypothesized structural relationships.

- This step allows researchers to assess unidimensionality, convergent validity, and discriminant validity.

- Convergent validity concerns whether indicators that are intended to measure the same construct are actually strongly related to that construct.

- Discriminant validity concerns whether theoretically different constructs are empirically distinguishable from one another.

- If the measurement model does not fit adequately, the researcher should investigate the source of the problem and consider theoretically justified respecification.

- Establishing an acceptable measurement model gives researchers greater confidence that the latent constructs have clear and stable meanings.

### Step 2: Evaluate the Structural Model

- Once an acceptable measurement model has been established, the second step is to evaluate the structural model.

- The structural model represents the hypothesized relationships among the latent constructs.

- Researchers can then determine whether the theoretical relationships among constructs are consistent with the observed data.

- Because measurement quality has already been evaluated, researchers can more clearly identify whether poor structural-model fit results from the hypothesized relationships rather than from measurement problems.

- Evaluation of the structural model also contributes to the assessment of nomological validity.

- Nomological validity concerns whether constructs relate to one another in ways that are consistent with the broader theoretical framework.

### Nested Models and Chi-Square Difference Testing

- Anderson and Gerbing recommend comparing a series of nested structural models.

- Nested models are models in which one model contains additional restrictions on parameters that are freely estimated in another model.

- The authors describe five structural models ranging from a null model with no structural relationships to a saturated model in which all relationships among constructs are estimated.

- The researcher’s theoretical model lies between these extremes and can be compared with theoretically plausible alternatives.

- Sequential chi-square difference tests are used to determine whether adding or removing structural relationships significantly changes model fit.

- These comparisons allow researchers to evaluate not only whether the proposed theoretical model fits but also whether alternative models provide a better or more parsimonious explanation.

### Why the Two Steps Are Separated

- Separating measurement from structural analysis helps researchers identify the source of model-fit problems.

- If no structural model could provide acceptable fit, the problem may indicate a more fundamental misspecification of the measurement model.

- With a one-step approach, researchers may not be able to identify whether poor fit originates in measurement or structural relationships.

- Evaluating the measurement model first also reduces interpretational confounding.

- The two-step approach provides a clearer basis for testing theoretical relationships because researchers know that the constructs have already demonstrated acceptable measurement properties.

## Advantages of the Two-Step Approach

- One major advantage of the two-step approach is that it separates measurement problems from structural-model problems.

- Researchers can determine whether poor overall fit is caused by inadequate measurement or by incorrect hypothesized relationships among constructs.

- The approach reduces interpretational confounding because the meaning of the latent constructs is established before structural restrictions are imposed.

- It allows researchers to evaluate convergent and discriminant validity before testing nomological validity.

- The two-step approach supports formal comparisons among the theoretical model and plausible alternative structural models.

- Comparing nested models helps researchers evaluate whether additional structural paths meaningfully improve explanation.

- The approach encourages researchers to consider parsimony by preferring a simpler model when additional parameters do not provide meaningful improvement.

- Paths that are hypothesized to be absent can also provide useful theoretical information when statistical tests support those restrictions.

- Adding more structural paths often improves goodness of fit, but doing so can reduce the strength of causal interpretation.

- The two-step approach therefore draws attention to the trade-off between improving model fit and maintaining theoretically meaningful restrictions.

- Another important advantage is that good fit in the measurement model cannot compensate for poor fit in the structural model, or vice versa.

- In a one-step approach, acceptable overall fit can potentially hide serious problems in one component of the model.

## Additional Considerations in Structural Model Interpretation

### Practical Versus Statistical Significance

- Anderson and Gerbing distinguish statistical significance from practical significance.

- The chi-square statistic is affected by sample size.

- With very large samples, statistically significant differences can occur even when the actual discrepancy between the model and the data is small.

- Researchers should therefore consider practical measures of fit in addition to formal significance tests.

- The normed fit index can provide additional information about how much observed covariance is explained by the model.

- A researcher may sometimes prefer a more parsimonious model even when a more complex model produces a statistically significant improvement if the practical improvement is very small.

### Cautions About Causal Interpretation

- Structural equation modeling does not automatically prove that relationships among constructs are causal.

- A model with acceptable fit is supported by the data, but it is not definitively confirmed.

- Other alternative models may also fit the same data.

- Temporal order alone is not sufficient evidence of causation.

- Researchers should also recognize the gap between an observed indicator and the latent construct it is intended to represent because indicators contain both measurement error and possible invalidity.

- Model respecification further limits the strength of causal conclusions because modifications may be influenced by characteristics of the particular sample.

- Cross-validation with a separate sample would provide stronger evidence for the model.

- In practice, sample-size requirements may make it difficult to divide a dataset into development and validation samples.

- For these reasons, causal interpretations from structural equation models should usually be stated cautiously and conditionally.

# Conclusion

- Anderson and Gerbing provide practical guidance for researchers using structural equation modeling for theory testing and construct validation.

- Their main contribution is the recommendation of a comprehensive two-step modeling approach.

- The first step evaluates and, when necessary, respecifies the measurement model.

- The second step evaluates the theoretical structural relationships after acceptable measurement has been established.

- The two-step approach allows researchers to test factor loadings, determine whether an acceptable structural model is possible, and formally compare the theoretical model with alternative models.

- It also allows researchers to improve the measurement model without compromising the later statistical evaluation of the structural model.

- By separating measurement and structural evaluation, researchers can make clearer and more theoretically meaningful interpretations.

- Structural equation modeling has substantial potential for theory development and construct validation when it is used carefully and researchers remain aware of the limitations of model fit and causal interpretation.

# References

Anderson, James C., and David W. Gerbing. 1988. “Structural Equation Modeling in Practice: A Review and Recommended Two-Step Approach.” *Psychological Bulletin* 103 (3): 411–423. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.103.3.411.
